weekLabel: Week 4 · Meeting A · Meet the Toolchain, Then Data as Evidence

slides.title: Three libraries, one trustworthy dataset
slides.subtitle: Meeting A · first contact with NumPy, pandas, and Matplotlib, plus the pandas trustworthiness interview
slides.teaching: Open by naming today's shift: Weeks 1-3 used only built-in Python; from today on, almost everything runs through a library someone else wrote and tested.

slides.title: A library is tested code you call, not code you rewrite
slides.statement: NumPy, pandas, and Matplotlib are third-party libraries - written and maintained by other people - that you import and call, the same way you already import pathlib and sys.
slides.supporting: Recall Weeks 1-3: import loads a module so its tools become available by name. Today's three libraries are installed separately but imported with the exact same keyword, import.
slides.teaching: Ask what 'third-party' should mean to a design student: someone outside this course wrote, tested, and maintains this code; our job is to call it correctly, not rebuild it.

outcomes.head: Compute
outcomes.body: Read a NumPy array's shape and dtype, select a value, and apply vectorized arithmetic.

outcomes.head: Bridge
outcomes.body: Recognize the same values as a pandas Series, then as columns inside a DataFrame.

outcomes.head: Call clearly
outcomes.body: Distinguish a function from a method, use a keyword argument, and read a lightweight docstring/type hint.

outcomes.head: Interview
outcomes.body: Run one pandas trustworthiness interview before filtering, deriving, or exporting data.

slides.teaching: Name the dependency chain: NumPy gives arrays, pandas adds labels, and Matplotlib shows selected evidence. The trustworthiness interview protects every later week.

items: NumPy first: array, shape, dtype, indexing, vectorization
Bridge the array into a pandas Series and DataFrame
Function vs. method, keyword arguments, and light documentation
Interview, clean, derive, and export Radley Hall data
slides.teaching: Tell students that Matplotlib appears only as a short preview today; Wednesday's studio makes the figure. Keep the focus on one connected data object moving through the toolchain.

slides.title: The library stack adds one capability at a time

steps.label: PYTHON
steps.head: Built-in logic
steps.body: Variables, conditions, loops, functions, and standard modules.

steps.label: NUMPY
steps.head: Numerical arrays
steps.body: Shape, dtype, indexing, and vectorized calculation.

steps.label: PANDAS
steps.head: Labeled evidence
steps.body: Series and DataFrames add names, indexes, and table operations.

steps.label: MATPLOTLIB
steps.head: Visible result
steps.body: Figures turn selected numerical evidence into an inspectable artifact.

slides.teaching: Trace one data value through the four layers. Introduce np, pd, and plt as conventional aliases when each layer is reached.

slides.title: NumPy arrays add shape, dtype, indexing, and vectorized arithmetic
slides.code:
import numpy as np

areas_m2 = np.array([35.0, 62.5, 44.2])
print(areas_m2.shape, areas_m2.dtype)
print(areas_m2[0])
print(areas_m2 * 10.7639)
slides.explainBody: shape says three values along one axis; dtype says they share a floating-point type; [0] selects the first value; multiplication acts on every element. This vectorized pattern is the numerical foundation under pandas columns.
slides.teaching: Trace each printed line before running it. Relate [0] to the list indexing students saw in Week 3B. Then contrast a vectorized multiplication with a loop: same conceptual operation, but the array owns the repetition.

slides.title: A Series is one labeled column of data
slides.definition: A Series is pandas' one-dimensional, labeled array: every value sits at an index position, the whole Series shares one dtype, and it can carry a name recording what it measures. A Series is the building block a DataFrame's columns are made of.

example.head: pd.Series([35.0, 62.5, 44.2], name='area_m2')
example.body: Three numbers - the same three from the NumPy array a moment ago. pandas labels them 0, 1, 2 automatically and remembers they are all area_m2; a plain NumPy array has neither label.

slides.note: The printed index (0, 1, 2) looks like a fourth column of data. It isn't - it's a label pandas assigned, and it never counts toward the Series' length or dtype.
slides.teaching: Introduce Series before running the code so students read the index correctly the first time; the code slide right after this one prints exactly this example. Verified: pd.Series([35.0, 62.5, 44.2], name='area_m2') prints a three-row Series indexed 0-2, dtype float64.

slides.title: Same three numbers, now as a Series
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

areas_m2 = pd.Series([35.0, 62.5, 44.2], name='area_m2')
print(areas_m2)
slides.explainHead: Read the index, then the values
slides.explainBody: The left column (0, 1, 2) is the index pandas assigned automatically - not a fourth data value. dtype: float64 confirms all three numbers share one type, and Name: area_m2 records what they measure, exactly as defined on the previous slide.
slides.teaching: Point at the index column on the left; it is not one of the three data values, it is a label pandas assigned automatically.

slides.title: A DataFrame is a table of Series sharing one index
slides.definition: A DataFrame is pandas' two-dimensional table: one or more named columns, each one internally a Series, all sharing the same row index. Almost every dataset this semester - including Radley Hall, later today - lives in a DataFrame.

example.head: pd.DataFrame({'room_id': [...], 'area_m2': [...]})
example.body: Two Series, room_id and area_m2, share row labels 0, 1, 2. rooms['area_m2'] pulls one column back out as exactly the Series from the previous slide - a DataFrame is Series bundled under one shared index, not a new kind of value.

slides.note: rooms['area_m2'] (one pair of brackets) returns a Series; rooms[['area_m2']] (two pairs) returns a one-column DataFrame. The bracket count changes the type you get back.
slides.teaching: Verified: rooms['area_m2'] returns <class 'pandas.Series'> and rooms[['area_m2']] returns <class 'pandas.DataFrame'> for the same column - confirm this contrast live if time allows, it is the single most common bracket-count slip beginners make with pandas.

slides.title: Two columns, one shared index: a DataFrame
slides.explainHead: Read the table, then find the Series inside it
slides.explainBody: rooms['area_m2'] is exactly the Series idea from the previous slide, now living inside a table alongside room_id, sharing its index. This is the structure you will use for almost every dataset this semester - including Radley Hall, later today.
slides.teaching: Ask which column is a Series by itself - point to rooms['area_m2'] as exactly the Series from two slides ago, just now inside a table.

slides.title: Matplotlib: turn numbers into a figure
slides.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

areas_m2 = [35.0, 62.5, 44.2]
energy = [58.0, 95.0, 71.5]
plt.scatter(areas_m2, energy)
plt.xlabel('area_m2')
plt.ylabel('energy_kwh_m2_yr')
plt.title('Three rooms')
plt.show()
slides.explainHead: No printed output - a figure instead
slides.explainBody: plt.scatter plots one point per room: x = area_m2, y = energy. plt.show() opens the figure window; it prints nothing to the console. Picture three dots, roughly left to right by area - does a bigger room always use more energy per square meter? We'll ask that question for real on Radley Hall's data in a few minutes.
slides.teaching: Warn students not to expect console output from this cell - a blank Console after Ctrl+Enter is correct here, the figure appears in the Plots pane instead. Quick recap before moving on: NumPy computes, pandas organizes, Matplotlib shows - one job each.

slides.title: Function call vs. method call

left.head: Function call (recall)
left.body: Recall from Weeks 1-3: a function is called by its own name, with data passed in as an argument - len(rooms), round(3.14159, 2).

right.head: Method call (new)
right.body: A method is a function that belongs to a specific object and is called with dot notation - rooms.head() reads 'call head on rooms.' The object comes first; that is the only new part.

slides.teaching: Write both forms on the board side by side: len(rooms) and rooms.head(). Ask which one exists because rooms is a DataFrame - method calls only make sense for the object they belong to.

slides.title: Same object, two ways to ask it a question
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

rooms = pd.read_csv('data/building_rooms.csv')

print(len(rooms))
print(rooms[['room_id', 'zone', 'area_m2']].head(2))
slides.output:
24
  room_id   zone  area_m2
0    R101  North     78.0
1    R102  North     44.2
slides.explainHead: len() is a function; .head() is a method
slides.explainBody: This is Radley Hall, this week's shared dataset - fictional, instructor-built data for this course, not measurements from a real building (more on that in a few minutes). len(rooms) is Python's built-in function, called on rooms exactly like the Week 1-3 examples. rooms.head() is a method - it belongs to the DataFrame and only exists because rooms is one. Both are completely ordinary; you will use both constantly.
slides.teaching: Ask what len(rooms) counts - rows, not columns or cells. Confirm against rooms.shape later this hour.

slides.title: A keyword argument names its value at the call site
slides.explainHead: Recall Week 3's default argument - now name it at the call site
slides.explainBody: allowance=0.10 is the default from Week 3. material_required(44.2, allowance=0.15) is new: writing allowance= at the call site overrides the default and makes the override self-documenting. You'll see this exact shape in pd.read_csv(path, sep=',') and df.to_csv(path, index=False) all semester.
slides.teaching: Note the float noise in 48.620000000000005 - same floating-point display quirk from Week 2, still true here. Not an error.

slides.title: A docstring documents what a function does, in place
slides.definition: A short, triple-quoted string as the very first line inside a function body - what it does, in one or two sentences. Week 3's area_status never had one; that's the gap we close today - from now on, every function you write gets one.

example.head: """Return required material area including a waste allowance."""
example.body: This line runs as ordinary code but does no calculation - Python stores it on the function. It can be read back later with .__doc__ or help(), the next slide's example.

slides.note: A docstring is not a # comment: a comment is stripped before running and cannot be read back; a docstring is stored on the function and stays readable by name after the fact.
slides.teaching: Tie directly to the critique that motivated this convention: earlier drafts required docstrings at Project 1 without ever teaching them; today is the week that closes that gap. Verified: material_required.__doc__ returns the exact triple-quoted string above.

slides.title: A type hint documents intent - Python never checks it
slides.definition: A note after a parameter's colon (area_m2: float) and after -> (-> float) stating the expected input and return type. Python does not enforce it - it documents intent for you, a teammate, or an AI assistant reading your code.

example.head: def material_required(area_m2: float, allowance: float = 0.10) -> float:
example.body: area_m2: float and allowance: float document the expected inputs; -> float documents the return. Nothing stops you from calling this with a string - Python still runs it, and fails later, if at all.

slides.note: "Does not enforce" is the one idea to hold onto: a type hint is a promise, not a guardrail. Project 1 grades whether the promise is present and accurate, not whether Python checked it.
slides.teaching: This is the single most common misconception with type hints. Verified: material_required('44.2', 0.10) raises TypeError inside the multiplication ('can't multiply sequence by non-int of type float'), not at the call - Python parses and calls the function fine, hints or no hints.

slides.title: One small function, fully documented
slides.code:
def rectangular_area(length_m: float, width_m: float) -> float:
    """Return rectangular floor area in square meters."""
    return length_m * width_m

print(rectangular_area(8.5, 5.2))
print(rectangular_area.__doc__)
slides.output:
44.2
Return rectangular floor area in square meters.
slides.explainBody: length_m: float and width_m: float document the expected inputs; -> float documents the return. Nothing stops you from calling rectangular_area('8.5', 5.2) - Python still runs it. The docstring is available any time via .__doc__ or help(). Starting today, every function you write in this course gets both.
slides.teaching: If time allows, actually run rectangular_area('8.5', 5.2) live and show the TypeError happens inside the multiplication, not at the call - the hint warned you, Python did not stop you.

slides.title: Meet Radley Hall - this week's shared dataset
slides.statement: Radley Hall is a fictional 24-room building, built for this course - not a real measured building.
slides.supporting: Weeks 4 through 7 all reuse this same room-by-room file, building_rooms.csv, so the analysis stays continuous across the month, the same way the Gallery/Lobby/Studio example carried through Weeks 1-3.
slides.teaching: Say plainly: no real building's performance data is behind these numbers. That claim matters as much as any code on the slide - provenance starts with saying what data is not.

slides.title: The same values gain structure as they move into pandas

steps.label: LIST
steps.head: Ordered values
steps.body: Python stores a simple sequence without a shared numerical dtype.

steps.label: ARRAY
steps.head: Numerical shape
steps.body: NumPy adds dtype, shape, vectorized arithmetic, and multidimensional indexing.

steps.label: SERIES
steps.head: One labeled column
steps.body: pandas adds an index and a column name to a one-dimensional array.

steps.label: DATAFRAME
steps.head: Related columns
steps.body: Several named Series share one row index as a table.

slides.teaching: Have students point to the index, one Series, and the full DataFrame. This visual dependency prevents pandas from appearing as an unrelated new syntax system.

slides.title: Load the real dataset with a keyword argument
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

rooms = pd.read_csv('data/building_rooms.csv', sep=',')
print(type(rooms))
slides.explainHead: sep=',' is the first keyword argument you'll use constantly
slides.explainBody: path is a positional argument - required, no name needed. sep=',' is a keyword argument: optional here (comma is already the default) but naming it makes the file format explicit for a reader. You'll see this same shape in df.to_csv(path, index=False) later today.
slides.teaching: Ask why naming an already-default argument is ever worth doing - answer: readability for a human, not necessity for Python.

slides.title: First question: how big is this?
slides.explainBody: rooms.shape is an attribute, not a method - no parentheses, because nothing needs to run; pandas already knows the size. The tuple reads (rows, columns): 24 rooms, 12 recorded fields. Always check shape before trusting a dataset's scale.
slides.teaching: Ask why there are no parentheses after shape - contrast with rooms.head(), which does something and therefore needs them.

slides.title: One interview checks scale, examples, types, completeness, and gaps
slides.callout: Run the five checks as one interview, then investigate any mismatch. A surprising dtype or count is evidence—not a display nuisance.
slides.teaching: Demonstrate the interview as one uninterrupted sequence. Have students predict what each check contributes before revealing the Radley Hall evidence. Emphasize that no single line is sufficient by itself.

slides.title: Third question: what do the first rows actually look like?
slides.output:
room_id   zone room_type  area_m2
0    R101  North     Lobby     78.0
1    R102  North   Gallery     44.2
2    R103  North    Office     18.5
slides.explainBody: head(3) returns the first 3 rows as a new DataFrame - a quick sanity check that column names, types, and values look like what the data dictionary promises. It is not a substitute for the dictionary itself.
slides.teaching: Point out the column subset in brackets - selecting fewer columns just to read them on a slide is a display choice, not a change to rooms itself.

slides.title: Commit to an answer before .info() runs
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: info() prints as a side effect and returns nothing, so x is None here - type(x) is NoneType, not a DataFrame, a string, or a dict.
slides.teaching: Poll all four options before revealing. A assumes info() hands back the DataFrame it summarized; B assumes the printed text IS the return value; D assumes a structured summary object comes back. Verified: type(rooms.info()) is NoneType, and the full summary text still prints once, before that line even evaluates.

slides.title: Fourth question: what does .info() summarize in one shot?
slides.output:
<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 24 entries, 0 to 23
Data columns (total 12 columns):
 #   Column            Non-Null Count  Dtype  
---  ------            --------------  -----  
...
 6   has_daylight      23 non-null     object 
 7   energy_kwh_m2_yr  23 non-null     float64
...
dtypes: float64(6), int64(1), object(1), str(4)
memory usage: 2.4+ KB
slides.explainBody: rooms.info() prints, in one call, the class, row count, every column's name, non-null count, and dtype, then a dtypes summary and memory usage - shape, dtypes, and head, all gathered in one place. Read Non-Null Count against the total, 24: has_daylight and energy_kwh_m2_yr both show 23, confirming the two gaps you already suspected. (The real printout lists all 12 rows; trimmed here to fit the slide - your own console will show every one.)
slides.teaching: Confirmed a moment ago: x = rooms.info() leaves x as None - the summary itself is a print side effect, not a return value. Also note pandas 3.0.5 prints the class as pandas.DataFrame, not pandas.core.frame.DataFrame as some older references show.

slides.title: A data dictionary and a provenance note are required artifacts

left.head: Data dictionary
left.body: One row per column: name, meaning, unit, allowed values. Written before you trust a single number - Project 1 requires one for every dataset you submit, starting with Radley Hall today.

right.head: Provenance note
right.body: Where did this file come from, when, and under what assumptions? For Radley Hall: an instructor-built fictional dataset for this course, not a measurement of a real building.

slides.teaching: Ask what would happen to a design decision built on a dataset with no provenance note - the answer is that no one downstream can tell fabricated data from measured data.

slides.title: Radley Hall's data dictionary (excerpt)
rows: room has at least one exterior daylight opening
slides.callout: Fictional, instructor-built data for this course - not measurements from a real building. Say so in your own provenance note whenever the data isn't yours.
slides.teaching: This excerpt covers 4 of 12 columns; Meeting B has students extend it to all twelve.

slides.title: Read rooms.isna().sum() one part at a time

parts.label: The DataFrame
parts.body: Already interviewed once - the same table shape and info() described a moment ago.

parts.label: Marks each cell
parts.body: A same-shaped True/False table - True wherever a value is missing.

parts.label: Adds down each column
parts.body: True counts as 1, so each column's total is its missing-value count.

slides.teaching: Trace the chain right to left: .sum() cannot run until .isna() has already produced a Boolean table for it to add. Verified: rooms.isna() returns a same-shaped DataFrame, all dtype bool; .sum() on it returns a Series of per-column counts, dtype int64.

slides.title: Fifth question: where exactly are the gaps?
slides.explainBody: isna() marks every missing value True; .sum() adds the Trues per column (True counts as 1). One missing has_daylight (room R303) and one missing energy_kwh_m2_yr (room R206) - now you know exactly where, not just that dtypes or info() looked odd.
slides.teaching: Connect directly back to the dtype table and info() a few slides ago - the object dtype and the 23-of-24 count were symptoms, isna().sum() is the diagnosis naming the exact rows.

slides.title: Both gaps, in one picture
slides.alt: Horizontal bar chart of missing-value counts per column; has_daylight and energy_kwh_m2_yr each show 1, every other column 0.
slides.caption: One bar per column of Radley Hall. Only two columns are not zero.
slides.explainHead: Two gaps, not a vague sense of dirt
slides.explainBody: The printed isna().sum() column is easy to skim past. Here the shape of the problem is immediate: 10 of 12 columns are complete, and exactly two rooms are missing exactly one value each. That is a small, nameable problem with a decision attached - not a reason to reach for dropna().
slides.teaching: Ask how this picture would change if someone had run rooms.dropna() first: both red bars would vanish, and so would two whole rooms. The gaps are the evidence that a decision is required.

slides.title: NaN as a modeling decision

left.head: NaN, defined
left.body: pandas' marker for 'no value recorded here' - not zero, not False, a genuine absence. It is exactly why has_daylight, expected to be a clean bool, prints as object instead.

right.head: Your decision, every time
right.body: Drop the row? Drop the column? Fill with an assumed value, and say so? Leave it and flag it? There is no default right answer - whichever you pick becomes part of your provenance note.

slides.teaching: Emphasize 'becomes part of your provenance note' - a silent drop is the one option that is never acceptable, because it erases the decision from the record.

slides.title: Filter to the rows that matter for a question
slides.explainBody: rooms['zone'] == 'South' produces a Series of True/False, one per row - Boolean comparison, recalled from Week 2. rooms[...] keeps only the True rows. 12 of 24 rooms sit in the South zone.
slides.teaching: Ask what south_rooms.shape would be if the comparison used 'south' in lowercase - answer: (0, 12), a common beginner mismatch worth naming.

slides.title: Add one derived column - don't overwrite the original
slides.explainBody: rooms['area_m2'] * 10.7639 multiplies every row's value at once - the same vectorized idea as the NumPy slide from the top of the hour. Assigning to a new column name (area_ft2) keeps area_m2 intact for anyone auditing your work later. The next slide adds a second derived column, this time wrapped in a documented function.
slides.teaching: Ask what would be lost if this line had instead written rooms['area_m2'] = ... - the original measured value, silently, under its original name. Meeting B's AI-audit exercise uses exactly this mistake.

slides.title: ...continued: a second documented function
slides.explainHead: Intensity and total answer different questions
slides.explainBody: Intensity is per square meter; energy_kwh_yr is a total. R306 has the highest intensity (410 kWh/m²/yr), yet its 8 m² area yields only 3,280 kWh/yr. A derived column changes which question the table can answer.
slides.teaching: Ask whether the small server closet must have the largest total because it has the largest intensity. The mismatch is the teaching point.

slides.title: Two rankings, two different answers
slides.alt: Two side-by-side horizontal bar charts of the top six rooms, one ranked by energy intensity where R306 leads, one by annual total where R306 is absent.
slides.caption: Left: ranked by intensity per square meter. Right: ranked by total annual energy. R306 leads one list and is missing from the other.
slides.explainHead: The derived column changes the ranking
slides.explainBody: R306 dominates the left chart at 410 kWh/m2/yr and does not appear on the right at all. Nothing about the data changed between these two panels - only which question was asked. This is what a derived column is for, and why naming it honestly matters.
slides.teaching: Point at R306 in the left panel, then ask the class to find it on the right before revealing that it is not there. The absence is the lesson.

slides.title: Export with a keyword argument you'll use every week
slides.explainBody: Without index=False, pandas writes its own row-number index as an extra unnamed column - clutter your collaborators didn't ask for. index=False is the keyword-argument habit Project 1 requires on every CSV you export, starting this week.
slides.teaching: Confirm the new shape is (24, 14) - two more columns than the raw file's 12, because area_ft2 and energy_kwh_yr were both added on the two previous slides.

slides.title: Studio check: would you trust this AI-suggested line?
slides.prompt: An AI assistant suggests rooms.dropna() right after loading - before anyone has looked at the data.
steps: Run the trustworthiness interview first: what does dropna() actually remove here?
Name which two rooms would silently disappear.
Decide: is a blanket dropna() ever the right first move?
Write the one-line policy you would use instead.
slides.teaching: dropna() with no arguments drops any row containing at least one NaN in ANY column - here that silently removes room R303 (missing has_daylight) and room R206 (missing energy_kwh_m2_yr), the same two gaps the isna().sum() interview just found. A defensible policy names which columns are required for the question at hand and only drops or flags rows missing THOSE columns, rather than accepting pandas default axis=0/how=any behavior as a shortcut. This is the same trustworthiness interview from earlier in the deck, now aimed at an AI suggestion instead of a human one.

slides.title: Typed columnar data changes scale—not the evidence rules

steps.label: CSV
steps.head: Read and exchange
steps.body: Transparent for small handoffs, but types and units still live outside the file.

steps.label: PARQUET
steps.head: Store typed columns
steps.body: Compressed columnar storage supports larger analytical tables and repeatable schemas.

steps.label: ARROW
steps.head: Move data efficiently
steps.body: A language-independent in-memory columnar format reduces conversion between tools.

steps.label: CONTRACT
steps.head: Preserve meaning
steps.body: Row meaning, units, null policy, identifiers, provenance, and checks remain mandatory.

slides.teaching: Optional current-practice bridge. Do not turn this into a format survey. The transferable idea is that faster storage and interchange do not repair an undefined row, ambiguous unit, or undocumented missing-value policy.

slides.title: A trustworthy table travels with a compact data contract

left.head: Machine-readable evidence
left.body:
Stable column names
Explicit dtypes and nullability
Persistent record identifier
Units or unit-bearing metadata
Schema and range checks

right.head: Human-readable evidence
right.body:
What one row represents
Who produced the data and when
Cleaning and exclusion decisions
Known gaps and intended uses
A reproducible run instruction

slides.teaching: Ask students which half their current CSV already supplies. The answer is usually neither in full. Connect this directly to the Project 1 README, data dictionary, flags, and validator.

slides.title: IFC, IDS, and Brick answer three different data-contract questions
rows: What asset objects, properties, and relationships are exchanged?
Validate schema/version, stable IDs, units, property sets, and the intended exchange view.
Which IFC information must be present, and which values are allowed?
Run the machine-readable requirement check; report failures instead of repairing them silently.
How are operational equipment, spaces, points, and their relationships named for analytics?
Check classes, units, relationships, and whether the same query transfers across buildings.
slides.callout: A pandas DataFrame is often an analysis view extracted from a richer building model. Keep the original identity, units, provenance, and requirement result so the table can be traced back to the asset evidence.
slides.teaching: Optional current-practice bridge. Keep the distinction crisp: IFC describes exchanged built assets; IDS specifies and checks required IFC information; Brick gives operational building data a portable semantic graph. Students are not expected to author these standards today—the transfer is that a CSV extract must not sever identity or provenance.

slides.title: Trustworthy data is interviewed, not just loaded
takeaways: Three libraries, three jobs: NumPy computes, pandas organizes, Matplotlib shows.
A method call belongs to an object; a function call does not - both can take keyword arguments.
Docstrings and type hints document intent; Python does not enforce the hint at runtime.
Before trusting a DataFrame, interview it: shape, dtypes, head, info, and NaN counts.
slides.teaching: Preview Meeting B: same dataset, but now students run every step themselves, document it, and add the NumPy + Matplotlib touch.
